fields.History: Early experiments identified a fat-soluble factor necessary for growth.
fields.What it does: Vision, immune function and normal cell development.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 900 mcg RAE men / 700 mcg RAE women
fields.When to take it: A meal containing fat is a practical choice.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 3,000 mcg RAE/day of preformed vitamin A. Excess preformed vitamin A is particularly important to avoid in pregnancy.

fields.History: Beriberi research linked illness to diets based on polished rice.
fields.What it does: Helps convert carbohydrates to energy and supports nerve function.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 1.2 mg men / 1.1 mg women
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour for routine intake.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: No U.S. upper limit established.

fields.History: Early nutrition researchers identified riboflavin while separating the B-complex factors.
fields.What it does: Supports energy metabolism through FMN and FAD coenzymes.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 1.3 mg men / 1.1 mg women
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour for routine intake.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: No U.S. upper limit established.

fields.History: Pellagra research helped establish niacin’s nutritional role.
fields.What it does: Supports energy metabolism and helps prevent pellagra.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 16 mg NE men / 14 mg NE women
fields.When to take it: Follow product directions. Prescription niacin has formulation-specific instructions.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 35 mg/day from supplements and fortified foods. High-dose forms can cause flushing or liver injury.

fields.History: Identified during early research on growth factors.
fields.What it does: Part of coenzyme A, which is involved in fat metabolism.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 5 mg adequate intake
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour for routine intake.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: No U.S. upper limit established.

fields.History: Distinguished from other B vitamins during early deficiency experiments.
fields.What it does: Supports amino acid metabolism, neurotransmitter production and hemoglobin formation.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 1.3 mg ages 19–50. After 50: 1.7 mg men / 1.5 mg women.
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour for routine intake.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: U.S. upper limit 100 mg/day. Long-term high supplemental intakes can damage nerves. Other authorities use lower limits.

fields.History: Research on diets containing raw egg whites helped explain biotin deficiency.
fields.What it does: Helps enzymes process fats, carbohydrates and amino acids.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 30 mcg adequate intake
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour. Tell your clinician and lab if you take biotin before a blood test.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: No U.S. upper limit established. Supplemental biotin can distort some lab results.

fields.History: Folate research grew out of studies of anemia, with early isolation work using leafy greens.
fields.What it does: Supports DNA synthesis and cell division. Folic acid before and during early pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 400 mcg DFE. Pregnancy and preconception guidance differ. See NIH.
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour. Preconception use is a life-stage issue.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 1,000 mcg/day of folic acid from supplements and fortified foods. High intake can obscure signs of B12 deficiency.

fields.History: Research into liver-based treatment for pernicious anemia led to identification of B12.
fields.What it does: Supports nerves, DNA synthesis and red blood cell formation.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 2.4 mcg
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour. Treatment and route depend on the cause of deficiency.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: No U.S. upper limit established. Metformin and acid-suppressing drugs can affect B12 status.
fields.Food sources: Fish, meat, dairy, eggs, fortified foods

fields.History: Citrus was used against scurvy before vitamin C was isolated.
fields.What it does: Supports collagen formation and improves nonheme iron absorption.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 90 mg men / 75 mg women. People who smoke need 35 mg more per day.
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour. Pair vitamin-C-rich foods with plant sources of iron.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 2,000 mg/day. High doses can cause diarrhea and cramps.

fields.History: Rickets research connected cod liver oil and sunlight with bone health.
fields.What it does: Supports calcium absorption and bone mineralization.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 15 mcg (600 IU) ages 19–70. 20 mcg (800 IU) over 70.
fields.When to take it: A meal containing some fat can improve absorption.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 100 mcg (4,000 IU)/day. Excess supplemental D can cause high blood calcium.
fields.Food sources: Fatty fish, fortified milk or plant beverages

fields.History: First identified as a dietary factor in animal reproduction experiments.
fields.What it does: Acts as an antioxidant and supports immune function.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 15 mg alpha-tocopherol
fields.When to take it: A meal containing fat is a practical choice.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 1,000 mg/day supplemental alpha-tocopherol. High doses can increase bleeding risk.

fields.History: Identified through experiments on blood clotting.
fields.What it does: Supports normal clotting and the activity of certain bone proteins.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 120 mcg men / 90 mcg women, adequate intake
fields.When to take it: A meal containing fat is a practical choice. If you take warfarin, keep intake consistent and discuss changes with your clinician.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: No U.S. upper limit established. Warfarin interaction is important.
fields.Food sources: Kale, spinach, broccoli, some fermented foods

fields.History: Bone mineral research established calcium as a major structural mineral.
fields.What it does: Supports bones, muscles and nerve signaling.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 1,000 mg for men 19–70 and women 19–50. 1,200 mg for women 51+ and men 71+.
fields.When to take it: Carbonate with food. Citrate with or without food. Absorption from supplements is highest at 500 mg or less at a time.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 2,500 mg/day ages 19–50 or 2,000 mg/day at 51+. Review medication spacing.
fields.Food sources: Yogurt, calcium-set tofu, sardines with bones

fields.History: Research on mineral nutrition identified magnesium as essential to enzyme activity.
fields.What it does: Supports muscle and nerve function and energy metabolism.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 400–420 mg men / 310–320 mg women, depending on age.
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour. Check timing with a pharmacist if using certain antibiotics or bisphosphonates.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 350 mg/day from supplements and medications. Food magnesium is excluded from this limit.

fields.History: Iron’s role in blood led to its use in treating iron deficiency anemia.
fields.What it does: Needed for hemoglobin and oxygen transport.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 8 mg adult men and women 51+. 18 mg women ages 19–50.
fields.When to take it: Separate individual calcium and iron supplements when practical. Vitamin C helps absorb nonheme iron.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 45 mg/day. Treatment doses can differ under supervision. Keep iron products away from children.

fields.History: Human deficiency research established zinc’s role in growth and development.
fields.What it does: Supports immune function, wound healing and taste.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 11 mg men / 8 mg women
fields.When to take it: Check spacing if taking certain antibiotics.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 40 mg/day. Excess supplemental zinc can cause copper deficiency.

fields.History: Iodized salt became a public health tool to prevent iodine deficiency.
fields.What it does: Needed to make thyroid hormones.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 150 mcg
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour for routine intake.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 1,100 mcg/day. Excess can disrupt thyroid function.

fields.History: Research established selenium as a component of protective enzymes.
fields.What it does: Supports thyroid hormone metabolism and antioxidant enzymes.
fields.U.S. daily intake: 55 mcg
fields.When to take it: No established preferred hour for routine intake.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: 400 mcg/day U.S. upper limit. Brazil nut selenium content varies widely.

nutrients.name: Omega-3 fats
nutrients.aliases: EPA, DHA, ALA, fish oil, algae oil

fields.History: Research identified essential fatty acids and later examined the roles of marine omega-3s.
fields.What it does: ALA is essential. EPA and DHA have different roles, and prescription omega-3 products can lower high triglycerides.
fields.U.S. daily intake: ALA adequate intake: 1.6 g men / 1.1 g women. No U.S. RDA for EPA or DHA.
fields.When to take it: Follow the product’s directions. Prescription formulations have their own dosing instructions.
fields.Upper limit and cautions: Review high doses with a clinician, especially with anticoagulants or a history of atrial fibrillation.
